questions.question: A pool has 8 workers, and each request needs 25 ms of worker time on average. What are the approximate pool capacity and utilization at 280 requests per second?
options: 320 requests per second and 87.5% utilization
200 requests per second and 140% utilization
8,000 requests per second and 3.5% utilization
280 requests per second and 100% utilization
questions.explanation: Each worker can complete about 1,000 / 25 = 40 requests per second. Eight workers provide about 320 requests per second, and 280 / 320 = 87.5%.

questions.question: Why can queue wait rise sharply before average utilization reaches 100%?
options: Monitoring creates extra requests
Bursts and slower requests find fewer free workers as headroom shrinks
A queue always doubles service capacity
Percentile latency is identical to average latency
questions.explanation: Near the capacity boundary, normal arrival and service-time variation more often finds every worker busy, so waiting grows nonlinearly.

questions.question: Checkout traces show 610 ms waiting to acquire a database connection and 42 ms executing the query. All 80 connections are busy with 146 waiters. What is the strongest current hypothesis?
options: The client network is the only bottleneck
Database connection-pool exhaustion is constraining the path
The query must be doing a full table scan
CPU is constrained because every slow request is compute-bound
questions.explanation: The long acquisition wait, full bounded pool, and queued callers directly connect request delay to connection-pool saturation; query execution itself is comparatively short.

questions.question: A team doubles application workers, but completed throughput and p95 latency do not improve under the same load. What should the team conclude?
options: The active constraint was not removed by adding workers
Every resource should now be doubled
The result proves CPU was the bottleneck
The baseline should be discarded
questions.explanation: A change to the active constraint should move the end-to-end outcome. No improvement means the hypothesis was wrong, the experiment was invalid, or another limit immediately dominated.

questions.question: How can retries worsen a bottleneck during a dependency slowdown?
options: They reduce attempted load to zero
They multiply attempted work while successful throughput may remain flat
They make every write idempotent automatically
They remove queue age from the system
questions.explanation: Retries add demand to an already slow path. Without bounded attempts, jitter, deadlines, and idempotency, they amplify queues and can duplicate unsafe work.

questions.question: What is the best verification after a targeted bottleneck fix?
options: Confirm one internal utilization graph fell
Rerun a comparable workload and compare the same user outcome, waits, errors, and downstream saturation
Increase all alert thresholds
Stop measuring because the bottleneck was found once
questions.explanation: Verification repeats the baseline conditions and checks the end-to-end outcome plus side effects. Bottlenecks move, so the next constraint must also be observed.
